metadata.title: Murphy v. United Parcel Service, Inc., 527 U.S. 516 (1999) (No. 97-1992)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Murphy v. United Parcel Service, Inc.

Opinion filed: 1999-06-22

Docket No.: 97-1992

Citations:
• 144 L. Ed. 2d 484
• 119 S. Ct. 2133
• 527 U.S. 516
• 1999 U.S. LEXIS 4370

Case holding summaries:
• "At most, petitioner has shown that he is regarded as unable to perform the job of mechanic only when that job requires driving a commercial motor vehicle — a specific type of vehicle used on a highway in interstate commerce."
• mechanic’s inability to obtain certification to drive commercial vehicles did not amount to a showing that employer regarded him as being unable to perform a class of mechanic jobs
• plaintiff not disabled where he could not perform a mechanic position that required that he drive a commercial motor vehicle, but where he could still perform other types of mechanic positions
• holding that Murphy, a truck driver, was not disabled under the ADA because his hypertension did not substantially limit his major life activities when he was medicated
• "At most, petitioner has shown that he is regarded as unable to perform the job of mechanic only when that job requires driving a commercial motor vehicle...."
• assuming arguendo that working qualifies as a major life activity
• "to be regarded as substantially limited in the major life activity of working, one must be regarded as precluded from more than a particular job."
• "[A] person is `regarded as' disabled within the meaning of the ADA if a covered entity mistakenly believes that the person's actual, nonlimiting impairment substantially limits one or more major life activities."
• holding that evidence of a plaintiff being "regarded as unable to perform only a particular job ... is insufficient, as a matter of law, to prove that petitioner is regarded as substantially limited in the major life activity of working"
• holding that the "determination of [a person's] disability is made with reference to the mitigating measures he employs."
• holding that an employee did not have a disability since the medication he took prevented his major life activities from being substantially limited
• hold- ing that "to be regarded as substantially limited in the major life activity of working, one must be regarded as precluded from more than a particular job"
• assuming that EEOC regulations are valid and applying them
• finding that the petitioner was not substantially limited in any major life activity where his high blood pressure was controlled by medication
• applying section 1630.2(j)(3) factors to "regarded as" claim
• holding that preclusion from mechanic job that requires commercial motor vehicle license not sufficient to show substantial limitation
• use of medication to correct high blood pressure
• stating that "to be regarded as substantially limited in the major life activity of working, one must be regarded as precluded from more than a particular job"
• applying section 1630.2(j)(3) factors to “regarded as” claim
• holding that preclusion from mechanic job that requires commercial motor vehicle license not sufficient to show substantial limitation
• "[T]o be regarded as substantially limited in the major life activity of working, one must be regarded as precluded from more than a particular job."
• "[T]o be regarded as substantially limited in the major life activity of working, one must be regarded as precluded from more than a particular job."
• concluding that summary judgment is proper where ADA plaintiff fails to show that he is "regarded as unable to perform a class of jobs"
• "[A] person is `regarded as' disabled within the meaning of the ADA if a covered entity mistakenly believes that the person's actual, nonlimiting impairment substantially limits one or more major life activities."
• negative side effects of hypertension medication might substantially limit a major life activity, but not reaching the issue because the petitioner did not seek certiorari on this question
• asking, in the context of the Americans with Disabilities Act, whether an individual’s impairment “substantially limits one or more major life activities” (internal quotation marks omitted)
• affirming summary judgment for employer where applicant was not precluded from a broad class of jobs, i.e., mechanics, but only from a particular job, i.e., mechanics required to drive commercial vehicles
• concluding that summary judgment is proper where ADA plaintiff fails to show that he is "regarded as unable to perform a class of jobs"
• "an individual claiming a disability under the ADA should be assessed with regard to any mitigating or corrective measures employed"
